1:
The timing is the first thing every witness notices. Keil and Delitzsch read the phrase after the plague as marking a completed sentence: with that last stroke the generation which came out of Egypt and was not to enter Canaan had been swept away entirely, so the ground was clear for a fresh muster. Ellicott says the same more briefly, that the plague probably carried off the remnant of those numbered at Sinai. Gill sets it before the war with Midian without fixing the interval, and Henry finds a mercy in the sequence — God had contended with them by a sweeping pestilence, and the ordering of a census at once shows he had not made a full end.

What the count was for is answered twice over. Keil and Delitzsch point out that it served the coming war but was chiefly a preparation for settlement, which is why the families within each tribe are enumerated here and were not at Sinai — the land was to be divided among families, not merely tribes. Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the other end: after thirty-eight years the tribes had to be regulated and the proportion of land ascertained, since although the whole was divided by lot, the lots were so disposed that a numerous tribe should not draw a small inheritance. Gill adds two further purposes, that it might appear all of the old generation were dead but two, and that God's faithfulness in multiplying them might be seen; Wesley makes the same double point, that the numbering demonstrates God both in cutting off those he had threatened and in a stupendous increase according to his promise.

Calvin turns that increase into the point of the chapter. In less than forty years the whole generation of military age had perished, and a single scourge had lately destroyed twenty-four thousand; who would not have expected the nation to be reduced by a quarter? That only two of the six hundred thousand survived is a memorable proof of God's anger — but that the people were so renewed by ordinary generation as to end the period at their former number is the work of inestimable grace. The promise to multiply Abraham's seed as the stars could not be allowed to be obscured at the very moment the other half of it, the gift of the land, was about to be fulfilled. God tempers his judgments so, Calvin says, that in the midst of indignation he remembers mercy; and that is precisely why the numbering follows the plague at once, so that it should be the more conspicuous how marvellously he had provided against any visible loss.

Calvin also queries the arithmetic of censuses. This is the second we read of in Moses, though from the tribute recorded in Exodus it must have been at least the third; and he thinks it likely that men gave in their names yearly or at stated times as they reached twenty, though a bare register would give no total without a comparison of the deaths.

Two smaller matters close the opening. Henry observes that Moses numbered the people only when God commanded — David did it uncommanded and paid dearly, God being Israel's king and not permitting so authoritative an act on any lesser warrant — and that Eleazar is joined in the commission as Aaron had been, which honoured him before the elders and confirmed his succession. Ellicott suspects a further arrangement not recorded here, the appointment of a head from each tribe to assist, as at the first census. Keil and Delitzsch note that the men Moses and Eleazar spoke with were the heads of the nation as the congregation's representatives, since they were the ones who would actually carry the count out, and that only the leading point of the instruction is preserved — the rest being simple enough to supply.
5:
Reuben heads the list as the eldest, and the figure attached to him is a loss. Gill counts four families and puts the decline since the last count at two thousand seven hundred and seventy, which he thinks the following verses exist to explain; Wesley gives the earlier total and lays the drop to Korah's conspiracy along with their other provocations. Ellicott adds the probable mechanism — Dathan and Abiram will have drawn many of their own tribesmen into the rebellion. Wesley defines the term being counted: these families are the chief houses, themselves subdivided into lesser ones.

Calvin sees two possible reasons for inserting the story here at all. Either it exalts God's grace, since after so great a loss the tribe was still numerous; or it explains a fact that would otherwise look strange, that other tribes outnumbered the one descended from Jacob's firstborn.

Whether Korah went down with them is the hard question of the passage, and it is a textual one. Ellicott reads the Hebrew as it stands — and Korah — and grants that on that reading he perished in the earthquake; but he notes that the Samaritan Pentateuch transposes the phrase and attaches it to the burning instead, so that the fire devoured Korah with the two hundred and fifty, and he suspects words may have dropped out here that stand in the fuller account. Clarke simply reports the Samaritan as not making Korah swallowed at all, and thinks that what in fact happened. Gill argues from the sense rather than the manuscripts, taking the words to mean the things belonging to Korah — his men and tents and goods — and placing Korah himself at the tabernacle door. Wesley sets both readings side by side and inclines the same way, with one careful exception in the list of what perished with him: his family, children excepted.

That exception is the point of the last verse, and it is stated flatly. Clarke admits the difficulty of squaring it with the earlier narrative, where the sons and the little ones seem to be swallowed, and resolves it by a close reading: in that verse only the wives and sons and little ones of Dathan and Abiram are actually named, so the children of Korah are not among those who perished. Gill explains why they were spared — they were not in their father's counsel, having either disliked the scheme from the first or repented and withdrawn from it — and Wesley puts it as a disowning, that they separated themselves from his tent and his company both.

Calvin makes the sparing more than a reprieve. It was no common mercy not merely to preserve them unhurt in the calamity but afterwards to raise shoots from an accursed root in whom God's spiritual riches would shine for the good of the church — since honourable mention is often made of that family, and it is likely that some of them wrote psalms and held the Spirit of prophecy at a time when possibly no priest had it. He calls this the profound abyss of God's various and unequal judgments, which it becomes us to adore with sober humility. Gill and Wesley both trace the same line forward to the singers of David's day and the psalms that carry their name.

One word in the account of the judgment carries more than it seems. Calvin notes that the term rendered a sign is properly a standard or banner, often used of something portentous that strikes the senses with astonishment and fills the mind with fear — which is why the story is repeated here, so that the manner of their death might stand as a perpetual example. Wesley says the same in plainer words: God made them a monument, to warn others against rebelling either against himself or against magistracy, and against usurping the priest's office.
12:
Simeon follows Reuben for two reasons, and Gill gives both: he was next by birth, and his tribe camped under Reuben's standard. The list of his sons does not quite match the older one, and the differences are noted rather than smoothed over. Gill points out two names spelt otherwise in Genesis and a third missing altogether; Keil and Delitzsch account for the missing one by saying Ohad left no family, and explain one of the variants as an interchange of two letters that is common in Hebrew. Wesley adds a general principle for the rest: such names might be added or changed on occasions the scripture does not record.

The figure is the most striking in the chapter. Wesley states it baldly — no tribe decreased so much, from fifty-nine thousand three hundred to twenty-two thousand two hundred, little more than a third of what it had been, with one whole family extinct in the wilderness. Gill and Ellicott look for the cause in the same place, the plague that had just been recorded: the chief offender in the matter of Baal-peor belonged to this tribe, and a prince setting that example is likely to have been followed by many of his own people. Gill passes on a rabbinic claim that goes further still, that the whole twenty-four thousand who died of the plague were Simeonites.

Ellicott follows the tribe's fortunes past the census. It is the only one on which Moses pronounced no blessing at all when he came to bless the tribes — a Greek manuscript inserting a clause to fill the gap — and in the division of the land its inheritance was no territory of its own but a remnant carved out of Judah's.

Gad is numbered third for the same reason Simeon was second, its place being under the same standard. Gill again registers the variant spellings, one of them wide enough to be a different name, and counts seven families. He guesses the tribe's loss was suffered in the presumptuous attempt on Canaan, when the people went up against God's will and were beaten back by the Amalekites — a conjecture the text does not confirm, but which at least looks for the cause where the chapter has been looking for it throughout, in something the men themselves did.
18:
Gad's total is five thousand one hundred and fifty short of what it had been, and Wesley marks the drop without explaining it. Ellicott offers an explanation, and it is more uncomfortable than the tribe-by-tribe accounts because it covers three tribes at once: Reuben, Simeon and Gad camped together on the south side of the tabernacle, and had probably contaminated one another by each other's example. All three come out of the wilderness smaller than they went in, and they are the three that shared a quarter.

Then Judah, and the arithmetic changes direction. Wesley marks the turn — about two thousand more than before, where every tribe named so far had been diminished. The list of sons carries its own history: Gill and Ellicott both note that two of them died in Canaan without children, so that two grandsons were substituted in their room to make up the families, which is why five names are counted where three sons survived.

Calvin makes that substitution the whole point of the passage. Of three sons two perished, a loss by which Judah might have seemed condemned to perpetual sterility; and the climax of an unparalleled mercy is that two of the children who remained were born of an incestuous connection, and from them grew the most numerous tribe in the register. The tribe that heads the camp and carries the promise is descended, on both counts, from a line that had every appearance of failing.

Issachar is taken next because he too stood under Judah's standard, and Gill gives the same kind of account as before: two names differently spelt from the older list, four families, and an increase of nine thousand nine hundred — the largest gain of any tribe so far, in a chapter which has to that point recorded almost nothing but losses.

The two verses are worth reading together for what they do to the shape of the register. The three tribes of the southern camp have just been counted and all three are smaller; the first two tribes of the eastern camp are counted here and both are larger, Judah by nineteen hundred and Issachar by nearly ten thousand. Nothing in the text draws the contrast, and none of the witnesses presses it beyond what each has said of the separate tribes; but Ellicott's explanation of the southern losses by shared quarters and shared example has its natural counterpart here, in a division that had kept its footing.
26:
Zebulun is numbered after Issachar for the same reason Issachar followed Judah, all three standing under one standard. Gill counts three families and an increase of three thousand one hundred, bringing the tribe to sixty thousand five hundred; Keil and Delitzsch note only that they answer exactly to the sons named in Genesis, which is as much as can be said of a list that raises no difficulty. With that the eastern camp is complete, and every one of its three tribes has grown.

Joseph is handled as two tribes, and Keil and Delitzsch explain the mechanism: his sons were born before the removal into Egypt and were raised into founders of tribes by Israel adopting them as his own. Gill notices what looks like an inversion in the order — Manasseh is named first although Jacob had preferred Ephraim and the standard belonged to him — and gives the reason as the census figures themselves rather than the birthright: Manasseh had by now the greater increase.

The house of Manasseh is set out in unusual depth, and its shape is peculiar. Keil and Delitzsch count eight families descending through a single son and a single grandson, six of them from that grandson's six sons, and observe that the genealogies elsewhere agree with this list save for one name that appears in a longer form in Joshua. Ellicott offers an explanation for the grandson's name from an unexpected quarter: his mother is said to have been an Aramitess, which would account for a boy called after the border country between Syria and Canaan.

Keil and Delitzsch also mark why the list runs down as far as it does. One of the six left no sons but five daughters, and their names are given here to prepare for the legal question their case would shortly raise. It is the one place in the register where the genealogy is carried past the point the count requires, and it is carried there because of an inheritance that would otherwise have had nobody to fall to. A muster of fighting men is not the obvious place to record five daughters; they are recorded because the division of the land, which is the other business of this chapter, would shortly turn on them.
34:
The increase in Manasseh is the largest in the chapter. Gill and Wesley both put it at above twenty thousand, taking the tribe from the smallest at Sinai to one of the most considerable, and Wesley reads it as the fulfilment of what Jacob had prophesied of Joseph's fruitfulness.

Calvin sets the two brothers side by side and finds the prophecy only half fulfilled. That Manasseh had a single son was already the beginning of Jacob's word that the elder should be inferior to the younger — and yet God's blessing so extended his family that it outgrew Reuben. On the other side, the numerousness in which Ephraim's descendants had been superior was itself a kind of type of the promised fruitfulness, but the excellency and dignity Jacob foretold was deferred to a distant time, since in this count Ephraim is smaller by about a third. God had not spoken in vain, Calvin says, though the fulfilment did not immediately appear.

Ephraim comes out of the wilderness eight thousand fewer than he went in, and Ellicott makes the loss the interesting thing about him. Jacob had foretold that this brother should be the greater; at the first census the Ephraimites were considerably the more numerous of the two and Ephraim carried the standard; and now, with Manasseh ahead by more than twenty thousand, Moses nevertheless renews and confirms the old prediction, assigning thousands to Manasseh but ten thousands to Ephraim. The prophecy is repeated at precisely the moment the numbers contradict it. Gill counts the families — three from sons and a fourth from a grandson, which Keil and Delitzsch confirm — and records the decrease without softening it.

Benjamin is numbered next as camping under Ephraim's standard, and his list has lost more than his brother's. Gill notes that five of the ten sons who went down into Egypt are simply absent, presumably having died without issue, and that of the five remaining names three differ from the older spelling; two further families descend from the eldest of them, making seven in all. Keil and Delitzsch give the same arithmetic — five families founded by sons and two by grandsons — and Wesley states the plain inference, that the missing five and their families were extinct. The tribe had nonetheless increased by ten thousand two hundred, which is the second largest gain in the chapter and comes from a stock that had lost half its names.
42:
Dan is the opposite case to Benjamin and everyone notices it. Keil and Delitzsch observe that his descendants formed a single family, named from an only son whose name appears in another form in Genesis, and that this list gives only the leading families into which the tribes were divided, so that smaller branches within it are passed over unnamed. Gill remarks on the disproportion — one family, and sixty-four thousand four hundred men in it, an increase of seventeen hundred. Wesley draws the comparison out and makes it the moral of the two verses: Dan's whole strength comes from one son and one family, while Benjamin, who had ten sons and five surviving families, musters fewer men — which shows that the increase of families depends singly on God's blessing and good pleasure, and not on the stock they start from.

Calvin adds a further reason for taking Dan as the standing case. He was contemptible among his brethren, so that it was an extraordinary blessing when Jacob said he should judge his people; and he is recorded as begetting only one son. Where the promise to Ephraim outran the number, the number here outruns anything the family tree would have led one to expect.

Asher is numbered next as standing under Dan's standard. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch agree that one of his sons founded no family and is therefore missing, and that two further families descend from a grandson, so that five are counted where four sons are named. The tribe had increased by nearly twelve thousand, which is the third largest gain in the register and the largest of any tribe outside the camps of Judah and Ephraim.

One detail in Asher's list is not like the rest, and both stop for it: a daughter is named. Gill supposes there must have been something remarkable about her — religion, or wisdom, or some particular grace — to be singled out so, and reports a further explanation from Maimonides, that she was an heiress: a stepdaughter whose own father left no sons, so that the inheritance was hers, exactly as it would afterwards be for the daughters of Zelophehad. It is the second time in the chapter that a woman's name is entered in a register of fighting men, and on Maimonides' reading both times for the same reason.
48:
Naphtali closes the list, and closes it on a loss. Gill notes that the tribe was numbered last of the twelve because it stood under Dan's standard with Asher, counts its four families, and puts the figure at forty-five thousand four hundred — eight thousand fewer than when they were first numbered, and the last of the five decreases the chapter records. Keil and Delitzsch add the one thing the list gives them occasion to say, that these four tally exactly with the sons of Naphtali named in Genesis and again in Chronicles — a plain agreement, in a register where several of the other tribes have required a note about a missing son or a variant spelling. Naphtali, Zebulun and Dan are the only tribes in the chapter whose family lists need no explaining at all, and of the three only Naphtali came out of the wilderness smaller. Nothing is said about why; where the losses of Simeon and Reuben are laid to particular sins and Gad's to a particular defeat, this one is simply recorded and left.

With that the twelve are complete, and Henry stands back from the whole register to say what the shape of it means. Dan had but one son, and yet that tribe is the most numerous of all except Judah — its beginning small and its latter end greatly increased; Benjamin brought ten sons down into Egypt, three of whose names have vanished, and the tribe is none of the largest. Providence, in the building up of families and nations, does not tie itself to probabilities: the barren hath borne seven, and she that hath many children is waxed feeble.

Henry is careful, too, about what the word family means in this chapter, since it is not what a modern reader would take it for. These are not households living together under one roof, but the descendants of one of the patriarchs' sons, who took his name and carried it in his honour. What is being counted is not a house but a line — which is why a tribe can consist of a single family and still muster sixty-four thousand men, and why the loss of a name from the list is the loss of a whole branch rather than of a household.
51:
The total is a decrease, and Clarke lays the two censuses side by side to show exactly how it comes about. Seven tribes gained some fifty-nine thousand between them, five lost sixty-one thousand, and the net figure after thirty-eight years is one thousand eight hundred and twenty fewer than at Sinai. He notices what the redistribution did not disturb. The same proportions hold between the four camp divisions as before, Judah's still the largest in the van and Dan's next in the rear — and both have been strengthened just as the nation is about to begin serious military operations, the leading division by nearly fifteen thousand men. He passes on a curiosity of Ainsworth's besides: the families of the twelve tribes number fifty-seven, which with the twelve patriarchs and their father makes seventy, the exact number of the souls that went down into Egypt.

What the figure means is where the comment turns. Calvin treats the sum as the proof of everything he has been arguing. Nature and reason would have predicted that only a remnant should enjoy the promised land, and if the inheritance had been restricted to a few the promise would have lain in obscurity; instead, within thirty-eight years in which more than six hundred thousand men had fallen, the same number stands again, short by some two thousand five hundred. A man must be blind four times over, he says, not to see in that mirror God's providence, the faithfulness of his gratuitous adoption, and his steadiness in keeping promises — while the survivors were at the same time plainly warned by so great a loss not to fall away again into superstition.

Wesley compresses the whole of it into one sentence: God manifested his justice in cutting off so vast a number, his mercy in supplying the loss so quickly, and his truth in both. Gill keeps to what the sum actually counts, the men of twenty years old and upward in the twelve tribes and fit for war.

Ellicott adds a reading from Bishop Wordsworth that turns the figure the other way. Under persecution in Egypt the Israelites multiplied exceedingly; after their deliverance they rebelled, and their days were consumed in vanity and their years in trouble. There is comfort in that for the church in affliction, and warning for it in days of prosperity.
52:
Henry answers the question the register raises before he does anything else. If any ask why such a particular account is kept of tribes and families and numbers, the reason is that as they were multiplied so they were portioned — not by common providence but by promise — and God will have the keeping of that promise noticed in both halves of it, the increase and the inheritance. He also notices what is not said. God does not tell Moses that by these the land shall be conquered; he takes the conquest for granted and says the land shall be divided, admitting the men just registered as heirs of Canaan by what amounts to a copy of the court roll. Calvin makes the same point from the demonstrative pronoun, which he thinks is used emphatically: unto these, lest anyone suppose the thing was still to be kept in store for a later generation. Registering a man was as good as putting the land in his grasp, and it was done precisely so that they should bestir themselves the more earnestly to go and take it.

Two rules govern the division and they pull against each other. The first is proportion, and Keil and Delitzsch state it plainly — a large tribe a large province, a small one a small, each according to the measure of its mustered persons. Gill notes that the instruction is given to Moses but was never for Moses, who would not enter the land at all; it was meant for his successor, and Henry says the same with a touch of pathos, that the man told how to give was to have none himself.

The second rule is the lot, and every witness treats it as the corrective to the first. Gill's reason for it is that the division should appear to come from God's determination rather than the judgment of a chief magistrate, however well he was bound by the rule of proportion. Henry puts it as a reservation: what seems left to a prince's prudence is finally reserved to the providence of God, in which they must all acquiesce however much it crosses their policy or inclination — as the God of nations reserves to himself the appointing of the bounds of our habitation, and as Christ, asked to assign the right hand and the left in his kingdom, acknowledged that it was not his to give.

How the two rules were reconciled in practice is worked out by Wesley. The lot decided which portion fell to which tribe, not how it was shared out within a tribe; that was left to the ruler's wisdom, by the proportion just laid down. Regard was had in the division to the goodness of the land as well as to its size; and if a portion proved too large or too small for the families it had to hold, part of it might be given to another tribe or taken from one — which is how Simeon and Dan came to hold ground out of Judah's share.

Clarke takes the word for the lot itself and follows it a long way. The Greek term became the ordinary name for a portion in spiritual things, so that an inheritance, and the persons appointed to a work, and at length the clergy, all take their names from it. Because the disposing of the lot was the Lord's, whatever fell out by providence came to be called a lot too. And the promised land divided this way is for Clarke a figure of a greater portion, given by God's good will to those who believe and obey — since it was unbelief that shut six hundred thousand out of the first inheritance, and these things happened for examples.
57:
Levi is counted apart, and the reason is the same one that governs the whole chapter. Keil and Delitzsch put it plainly: the muster was taken with the conquest of Canaan in view, and this tribe was to receive no territory, so it stands outside the reckoning — as it had at Sinai. Henry draws out what that exemption cost and what it saved. Levi had no inheritance with the rest, and so was not numbered with them; but because it was not numbered with them it never came under the sentence passed on all who were, so that Eleazar and Ithamar, and presumably others already grown, did enter the land. Even so, he notes, the tribe had increased by only a thousand in thirty-eight years and remained one of the smallest.

The list of families is deliberately incomplete. Gill goes through the gaps one by one — a son of Gershon missing, two of Kohath's sons absent, only one of the lines descending from Korah named — and reports the ordinary explanation, that these men either had no sons or their descendants failed. Keil and Delitzsch say the enumeration is simply broken off, and give the reason: it turns aside to trace the descent of Moses and Aaron, which is what the passage is really for.

Calvin finds two things worth remarking in that genealogy. The first is that among Levi's sons the priestly family descends from the one named last, which suggests that the law of primogeniture was not consulted when God chose where to take his priests. The second is the naming of a mother, which scripture does not usually do. It cannot be family pride, since Moses records in the same breath that he and his own children were passed over for the priesthood; Calvin thinks rather that he is refusing to conceal something discreditable, in order to set God's indulgence higher — for on the plain reading his parents' marriage was within a forbidden degree. He adds the historical mitigation: the practice was so general among the eastern nations that no one then reckoned it unlawful, and the prohibition had not yet been given.

Ellicott records that the difficulty has been felt and answered another way. Some have supposed the woman named to be a granddaughter or a remoter descendant of Levi, and the Amram who fathered Moses to be a different man from Kohath's son; he cites authorities on both sides without settling it, noting only that the Hebrew here omits its subject as it does elsewhere.

The deaths of Aaron's two elder sons are brought in again, and both Henry and Calvin explain the repetition. Henry sets it beside the earlier recalling of Korah's punishment — these things happened for examples. Calvin sees more at stake than a warning. With two of four sons cut off by a sudden death the high priesthood hung on two lives, and the history is repeated so that God's providence in preserving an order on which the safety of the whole church depended should be the more clearly seen. He finds the numbers themselves remarkable in the same direction: twenty-three thousand Levites, and the priestly line issuing from two heads only. God raises his church by means unknown to men, that his power may be magnified in weakness — and the cause of that death is recorded once more so that priests may beware not only of wilful sacrilege but of error and negligence.
63:
The chapter ends by checking one register against another. Henry supposes that particular directions must have gone out to the men taking the count in each tribe, to compare the new rolls with the old and see whether a single name survived from Sinai — and that not one did, save the two. Keil and Delitzsch describe the closing verses as a formula noting that the penal sentence pronounced years before had now been carried out to the letter. Calvin observes the one change between the two counts that makes the comparison possible at all: the first was taken by Aaron, this one by Eleazar, and the difference is specified so that Moses may take the occasion to commemorate the judgment.

Calvin will not let that judgment be explained away as ordinary mortality. It might be objected that most of those men would have died naturally, having been thirty or forty or fifty at the start and so near eighty by the end; he grants the point as far as it goes. But many had not reached their twenty-fourth year, and not a few were younger than Caleb and Joshua, who were alive and vigorous for many years afterwards. It was not old age but God's vengeance that cut off half of them by an untimely death, as though he had visibly put forth his hand from heaven. Moses records that they died exactly as God had said, Calvin adds, not only to teach us fear but to teach us to be roused in earnest by threats.

Henry finds three things in the same fact. The righteousness of God, and his faithfulness to his own threatenings — better all those carcasses should fall than the word of God, and those whom he has condemned cannot escape either by losing themselves in a crowd or by the delay of the sentence, since many of the guilty survived almost to the last of the forty years and were still gone before this muster. The goodness of God, in raising a generation as numerous as the one cut off, so that the name of Israel should not fail and the inheritance not be lost for want of heirs. And the truth of God in keeping the particular promise made to two men.

He also notices an advantage the new generation had over the old. They were all middle-aged, between twenty and sixty, in the prime of their time for service; and through the thirty-eight years of wandering they had leisure to acquaint themselves with the law, having neither civil nor military business to divert them, with Moses and Aaron to teach them and God's good Spirit given to instruct them.

One qualification is entered on the sentence, and it concerns Levi. Gill points out that the comparison is with the numbering of Israel and not of the Levites, several of whom were living still; Wesley states the reason flatly, that they were not guilty of that sin and so did not share the judgment. Ellicott is less certain. He notes that the statement of fulfilment comes after the Levite total rather than before it, which might suggest the exclusion covered that tribe too, while the clause explaining why they were not numbered with the rest can be urged the other way — and he leaves the two considerations standing against each other.
